passage.bullet: 218 London merchants pooled £68,000 → funded armed galleons without draining royal taxes
Ships carried silver bullion and English broadcloth → opened direct trade with Asian spice markets
James Lancaster returned with pepper and cotton → delivered over 300% profit for investors

context.bullet: Portuguese and Dutch spice fleets dominated Asia → England risked exclusion from eastern wealth
Costly war with Catholic Spain strained royal funds → Elizabeth favoured private joint-stock ventures

stems.stem: On New Year's Eve 1600, Elizabeth I granted a monopoly charter to ____________ who pooled ____________ to fund eastern voyages.
Trading silver bullion and broadcloth for ____________ allowed ____________ to generate profits exceeding ____________.
Granting exclusive trading rights helped England challenge ____________ without spending scarce ____________.

lesson_1.watch_out: The East India Company began in 1600 as a private joint-stock trading syndicate, not a department of the British government or an army of conquest.

passage.bullet: Ambassador Sir Thomas Roe negotiated with Emperor Jahangir → won an imperial decree for Surat
Fortified trading warehouses called factories rose at Surat, Madras, Calcutta, and Bombay
Company merchants recruited armed Indian infantry called sepoys → turned depots into corporate fortresses

context.bullet: Mughal India produced a quarter of world goods → English traders arrived as humble petitioners
Armed Dutch and Portuguese rivals patrolled Indian seas → Company depots needed heavy coastal defences

stems.stem: Sent by King James I in 1615, diplomat ____________ persuaded Mughal Emperor ____________ to permit English trade at ____________.
Throughout the seventeenth century, fortified warehouses known as ____________ expanded across key ports including ____________.
Recruiting local Indian soldiers called ____________ transformed commercial depots into ____________.

lesson_1.watch_out: Seventeenth-century Company factories were fortified coastal warehouses run by merchant agents called factors, not industrial steam mills with machinery.

passage.bullet: Company merchants mounted heavy cannons on Fort William without permission → defied Bengal's ruler
Nawab Siraj ud-Daulah marched 50,000 troops on Calcutta → captured Fort William inside three days
British writers sensationalized suffocation deaths in the Black Hole guardroom → fuelled calls for conquest

context.bullet: Central Mughal authority weakened after 1707 → regional Nawabs guarded Bengal's rich textile revenues
Warring British and French traders fortified Indian ports → alarmed Siraj over foreign military meddling

stems.stem: Defying local authority, British merchants mounted ____________ around ____________ without the Nawab's consent.
To assert his sovereignty over Bengal, ____________ marched ____________ against Calcutta and seized the fort.
Overnight deaths inside the ____________ guardroom were exaggerated in Britain to justify ____________.

lesson_1.watch_out: Siraj ud-Daulah did not attack Calcutta unprovoked—he marched to stop a foreign trading company illegally mounting heavy artillery inside his sovereign province.

passage.bullet: Outnumbered Robert Clive bribed Bengali commander Mir Jafar with gold and the Nawab's throne
Tarpaulins kept British gunpowder dry during monsoon rain → drenched Siraj's exposed cannon powder
Mir Jafar's divisions stood motionless on 23 June → British artillery shattered Siraj's loyal troops

context.bullet: Wealthy Jagat Seth bankers resented Siraj's taxes → financed Clive's plot to install a puppet ruler
Trained coastal sepoy battalions backed Clive's redcoats → turned corporate guards into a field army

stems.stem: Outnumbered on campaign, Robert Clive secretly promised ____________ the Nawab's throne in exchange for ____________.
During the June downpour, British crews covered their gunpowder with ____________ while Siraj's cannons ____________.
Because traitorous divisions stood ____________ during battle, Company artillery shattered ____________ and installed a puppet Nawab.

lesson_1.watch_out: Plassey was won primarily through political conspiracy, Indian banker backing, and Mir Jafar's treason rather than superior British military numbers.

passage.bullet: Defeated Emperor Shah Alam II signed the 1765 Treaty of Allahabad after losing at Buxar
Winning the Diwani gave Company clerks sovereign tax control across Bengal, Bihar, and Orissa
Relentless peasant tax collection during drought → triggered the 1770 famine, starving ten million people

context.bullet: Bengal land taxes now paid for Indian goods → ended Britain's need to ship silver
Famine horrors and corrupt Company nabobs shocked London → sparked later Tea Act bailouts

stems.stem: Following victory at Buxar, Emperor ____________ surrendered the ____________ across Bengal, Bihar, and Orissa.
Instead of trading silver for goods, Company agents extracted ____________ directly from ____________.
Unbending tax collection during severe drought caused the ____________, starving an estimated ____________ while profits rose.

lesson_1.watch_out: The 1770 Bengal famine was not merely a natural drought—relentless East India Company tax extraction stripped villages of grain reserves needed to survive.

passage.bullet: Liverpool and Bristol ships carried guns, iron, and cloth → traded in West Africa for captives
Captains forced kidnapped Africans across the Atlantic → sold survivors onto brutal colonial plantations
Vessels returned carrying slave-grown sugar, rum, tobacco, and cotton → enriched British banks and ports

context.bullet: Soaring European demand for sweetened tea and coffee → drove ruthless Caribbean plantation expansion
Birmingham gunsmiths and Lancashire weavers supplied trade goods → tied domestic industry to slavery

stems.stem: Departing from ports such as ____________, merchant ships traded manufactured ____________ along the West African coast.
Captive Africans were transported across the Atlantic and sold into ____________ across the Americas.
Returning holds filled with ____________ generated vast fortunes for ____________ across Britain.

lesson_2.watch_out: Triangular trade was not a distant colonial sideline—profits from enslaved labour directly financed British banks, factories, and port cities like Liverpool and Bristol.

passage.bullet: Charles II and James, Duke of York chartered the Royal African Company monopoly in 1672
Armed West African forts imprisoned captives branded RAC with hot irons → enforced corporate ownership
Winning the 1713 Spanish Asiento treaty → made Britain the leading supplier to Spanish America

context.bullet: Parliament ended the company monopoly in 1698 → private Bristol and Liverpool slavers surged
Victory in the War of the Spanish Succession → handed Britain lucrative Atlantic trade concessions

stems.stem: Backed directly by King ____________ and the Duke of York, the ____________ held a royal monopoly from 1672.
Inside armed West African forts, agents branded captives with the letters ____________ to mark ____________.
Securing the ____________ contract in 1713 gave British merchants exclusive rights to supply ____________.

lesson_2.watch_out: Transatlantic slave trading was not carried out solely by rogue pirates—the Stuart royal family personally led and profited from the Royal African Company.

passage.bullet: Hundreds were chained onto cramped wooden shelves → allowed less space than a coffin
Suffocating, filthy holds spread seasickness, fevers, and dysentery across the eight-week voyage
Roughly one in six captives perished at sea → crews threw dead bodies overboard

context.bullet: Captains feared African uprisings at sea → enforced iron shackles, nets, and brutal deck punishments
Even after Dolben's 1788 ship regulation, the Brookes still legally crammed over 450 captives aboard

stems.stem: Throughout the eight-week crossing, captives lay locked in ____________ upon wooden shelves with less space than ____________.
Pitch-black, airless decks bred rampant ____________ and ____________ among chained prisoners.
Brutal overcrowding meant roughly ____________ died during the voyage before reaching the Americas.

lesson_2.watch_out: Enslaved Africans did not remain passive during the Middle Passage—crews used heavy iron shackles and deck barricades precisely because shipboard revolts were frequent.

passage.bullet: Navigational errors left the Zong short of water → sickness spread rapidly through packed holds
Collingwood drowned 133 sick captives over three days → owners claimed maritime cargo insurance
Abolitionist Granville Sharp publicized the courtroom scandal → exposed chattel slavery's legal inhumanity

context.bullet: Insurers paid nothing for natural deaths → perverse legal rules rewarded throwing sick captives overboard
Olaudah Equiano alerted Granville Sharp to the Liverpool insurance trial → sparked abolitionist outrage

stems.stem: After navigational errors caused a severe ____________, sick captives aboard the Zong threatened ____________.
Captain Collingwood ordered ____________ drowned so Liverpool owners could claim ____________ for jettisoned cargo.
Campaigner ____________ exposed the massacre in court, proving English law treated human beings as ____________.

lesson_2.watch_out: No crew member of the Zong was ever prosecuted for murder—the 1783 London court case was strictly a civil dispute between slave-ship owners and insurance underwriters.

passage.bullet: Mass-printed Brookes ship diagrams showed bodies stowed like timber → shocked British readers visually
Freed author Olaudah Equiano published his bestselling 1789 autobiography → gave first-hand African testimony
Nationwide petitions and sugar boycotts pressured MPs → Parliament passed the 1807 Abolition Act

context.bullet: Haitian and Jamaican slave revolts raised military costs → weakened planter resistance in Parliament
Outlawing slave ships in 1807 left Caribbean plantation slavery legal until final abolition in 1833

stems.stem: Mass-produced prints of the ____________ revealed how human beings were packed like ____________ below deck.
Through his bestselling autobiography, ____________ shattered pro-slavery myths with first-hand testimony of ____________.
Sustained public pressure finally forced Parliament to pass the ____________, banning ____________ on British ships.

lesson_2.watch_out: The 1807 Abolition Act banned the transatlantic slave trade on British ships, but it did not free people already enslaved on Caribbean plantations until 1833.

passage.bullet: Oliver Cromwell's 1655 fleet invaded Spanish Jamaica → shattered colonial control across the island
Enslaved Africans seized wartime chaos to escape → retreated into steep Blue Mountain rainforests
Self-liberated Maroons grew communal crops and drilled fighters → defended independent mountain strongholds

context.bullet: Repelled from Spanish Hispaniola first, Cromwell's commanders seized lightly defended Jamaica as consolation
Jamaica soon overtook Barbados as Britain's richest sugar colony → intensified clashes with free Maroons

stems.stem: During Oliver Cromwell's 1655 ____________ campaign, English forces captured ____________ from Spain.
Amid the chaos of conquest, formerly enslaved Africans fled into the ____________ to establish ____________.
Known as ____________, these free communities sustained themselves by farming ____________ and training militia units.

lesson_3.watch_out: Jamaican Maroons did not wait to be granted freedom by Europeans—they liberated themselves during the 1655 invasion and defended sovereign towns for over eighty years.

passage.bullet: Field gangs cut cane from dawn until dusk in tropical heat under overseers' whips
Exhausted mill workers laboured eighteen-hour harvest shifts → risked limbs in iron crushing rollers
Relentless overwork and violence caused soaring deaths → absentee planters imported fresh captives yearly

context.bullet: Spoiling cut cane needed immediate crushing and boiling → imposed factory-style schedules before industrialisation
Rich planters lived in grand British country houses → left ruthless Jamaican overseers chasing output

stems.stem: Driven by overseers' cowhide whips, enslaved field gangs toiled in ____________ from ____________.
Eighteen-hour harvest shifts inside sugar mills exposed exhausted workers to ____________.
Because extreme exhaustion caused ____________, wealthy absentee planters continually imported ____________ via the Middle Passage.

lesson_3.watch_out: Sugar plantations were not simple farms—they operated like deadly agro-industrial factories where fast cane processing combined heavy field labour with dangerous mill machinery.

passage.bullet: Workers snapped tool handles, damaged copper boiling cauldrons, slowed pace, and feigned sudden illness
Communities preserved West African spiritual practices, herbal healing, and hopeful music inside slave quarters
Elders told nightly Anansi spider stories → celebrated outwitting powerful oppressors through sharp intelligence

context.bullet: Jamaican slave laws punished open rebellion with torture → made covert daily sabotage vital
Many captives came from Gold Coast Akan societies → carried Anansi folklore into Caribbean culture

stems.stem: To disrupt planter profits without triggering execution, field hands deliberately ____________ and damaged ____________.
Inside the quarters at night, enslaved families defended their humanity through West African ____________ and ____________.
Recounting ____________ tales inspired resilience by showing how a small creature outsmarted ____________.

lesson_3.watch_out: Resistance was not limited to armed uprisings—covert workplace sabotage and preserving West African culture were vital daily weapons against dehumanisation.

passage.bullet: Asante leader Queen Nanny united eastern Windward Maroons through disciplined command and spiritual authority
Fighters disguised themselves in living forest branches → ambushed marching redcoats along narrow mountain trails
Signallers blew cow-horn abeng calls across misty ridges → coordinated rapid guerrilla strikes

context.bullet: Scarlet coats and heavy muskets slowed British troops → exposed columns to jungle ambushes
Maroon raids freed captives and seized weapons → halted British sugar expansion across eastern Jamaica

stems.stem: In eastern Jamaica, Asante strategist ____________ trained Windward fighters to blend into ____________ using living branches.
Sounding the ____________ across steep ridges allowed Maroon lookouts to coordinate ____________ miles apart.
Hit-and-run ambushes in dense rainforest repeatedly routed ____________ trained only for open European battlefields.

lesson_3.watch_out: Queen Nanny was a real historical Asante leader documented in colonial Jamaican dispatches, even though British officials tried to dismiss her authority as witchcraft.

passage.bullet: Costly jungle defeats forced Governor Edward Trelawny to seek a white-flag truce in 1739
Treaty terms recognized Maroon freedom and granted 1,500 sovereign acres of mountain land
Maroon leaders agreed to return future plantation runaways → protected autonomy through painful compromise

context.bullet: Cudjoe signed for Leeward Maroons in 1739 before Windward towns accepted similar terms in 1740
Closing mountain refuge routes stabilized Jamaican sugar estates → deepened divisions between Maroons and captives

stems.stem: Exhausted by decades of guerrilla defeats, Governor ____________ formally recognized Maroon freedom and ____________.
Yet the treaty carried a tragic price because Maroon leaders promised to ____________.
Winning a signed peace proved that organized African resistance could force ____________ to negotiate.

lesson_3.watch_out: The 1739 treaty secured real freedom for existing Maroon communities, yet it deliberately stabilized plantation slavery by cutting off mountain sanctuary for new runaways.

passage.bullet: Seven Years' War victory left Britain £133m in debt → London sought cheaper frontier defence
George III's 1763 Proclamation banned settlement west of the Appalachians → angered land-hungry colonists
Quartering Acts forced colonial towns to house 10,000 redcoats → fuelled fears of military control

context.bullet: Indigenous alliances led by Pontiac attacked western forts in 1763 → prompted London's boundary line
Expelling France from Canada removed a shared enemy → colonists needed British protection far less

stems.stem: Burdened by a ____________ war debt after 1763, King George III sought to avoid costly frontier clashes with ____________.
Drawing the Proclamation Line along the ____________ outraged settlers who expected access to ____________.
Resentment deepened when the ____________ forced colonial towns to house ____________ in peacetime.

lesson_4.watch_out: Winning the Seven Years' War ironically weakened Britain's hold on America—removing French Canada made colonists less reliant on British troops just as London demanded higher taxes.

passage.bullet: Colonists elected zero Westminster MPs → argued Stamp Act taxes violated freeborn English rights
Sons of Liberty burned tax offices and hung effigies → forced royal stamp collectors to resign
Coordinated boycotts crippled British manufacturing exports → pressured Parliament into repealing the tax in 1766

context.bullet: Unlike earlier port customs duties, stamps taxed everyday colonial newspapers, wills, and playing cards
Parliament repealed the Stamp Act in 1766 yet asserted full power to legislate over colonies

stems.stem: Taxing everyday items such as ____________ provoked fury because colonists held no seats in ____________.
Radical groups called the ____________ intimidated officials while merchants organized ____________ across colonial ports.
Slumping British trade hurt London merchants so badly that MPs voted to ____________ in 1766.

lesson_4.watch_out: Colonists did not protest merely because stamps were expensive—they feared accepting any internal tax passed without elected colonial representatives would destroy self-government.

passage.bullet: Panicked redcoats pelted with ice and oyster shells fired into a crowd, killing five
Paul Revere's print showed an officer ordering deliberate volleys into peaceful citizens → hid crowd disorder
Mass-printed engravings turned Crispus Attucks and four others into martyrs → inflamed anti-British fury

context.bullet: Four thousand redcoats occupied Boston to enforce customs duties → sparked daily street clashes
Future Patriot John Adams defended the accused soldiers in court → most won acquittal

stems.stem: What began on 5 March 1770 with crowds throwing ____________ ended when panicked soldiers killed ____________, including Crispus Attucks.
Silversmith ____________ circulated a dramatic engraving depicting redcoats firing an ordered volley into ____________.
Framing the chaotic shooting as a premeditated ____________ united colonists against ____________.

lesson_4.watch_out: Paul Revere's famous print is propaganda rather than an accurate eyewitness record—it erased the snowballs, clubs, and confusion to portray an ordered execution.

passage.bullet: Parliament let the struggling East India Company ship 18m pounds of surplus tea direct
Direct corporate sales undercut smuggled Dutch tea and cut out independent colonial merchants
Buying cheaper Company tea still paid Townshend tea duty → conceded Parliament's right to tax

context.bullet: Famine in Bengal crashed East India Company revenues → connected Indian plunder to Boston protests
Colonial traders feared Parliament might next hand corporate monopolies over all American commerce

stems.stem: Designed to rescue the ____________ from 18 million pounds of unsold stock, the 1773 Act granted a ____________.
Even though tea prices fell, shipping direct to chosen agents bypassed ____________ across American ports.
Purchasing the discounted cargo meant silently accepting ____________ without colonial consent.

lesson_4.watch_out: The 1773 Tea Act actually made legal tea cheaper for Americans, not dearer—colonists rebelled against corporate monopoly and the hidden Parliamentary tax principle.

passage.bullet: Disguised Sons of Liberty dumped 342 chests worth £10,000 into Boston harbour on 16 December
Parliament's 1774 Coercive Acts closed Boston port until colonists repaid the East India Company
Crown law stripped Massachusetts of elected self-government → drove all thirteen colonies toward revolution

context.bullet: Rather than isolating Boston, harsh punishment prompted twelve colonies to convene the First Continental Congress
General Thomas Gage took command of Massachusetts → replaced civilian politics with martial confrontation

stems.stem: Furious after disguised protesters destroyed ____________ worth of Company cargo, King George III demanded harsh retaliation.
Through the 1774 ____________, Parliament blockaded ____________ and abolished Massachusetts self-government.
Instead of intimidating New England into submission, collective punishment united ____________ toward armed resistance.

lesson_4.watch_out: London intended the 1774 Coercive Acts—called the Intolerable Acts in America—to isolate radical Massachusetts, yet the crackdown rallied the other twelve colonies behind Boston.

passage.bullet: Redcoats marched to seize Concord weapon stores → triggered deadly militia gunfire at Lexington Green
Governor Dunmore promised freedom to enslaved people fleeing rebel masters to fight for George III
Thousands of Black volunteers joined British lines → pushed southern slaveholders firmly into rebellion

context.bullet: Dunmore's Black soldiers wore sashes reading Liberty to Slaves → fought for self-emancipation, not empire
Dunmore freed only runaways from Patriot rebels → enslaved workers owned by Loyalists stayed chained

stems.stem: When British soldiers marched toward ____________ to seize weapons in April 1775, bloodshed erupted at ____________.
Later that year, Virginia's royal governor issued ____________, offering liberty to enslaved people who fled ____________.
Seeing thousands of Black workers join Crown forces drove furious ____________ into full rebellion.

lesson_5.watch_out: Lord Dunmore was not a moral abolitionist—his 1775 proclamation was a military tactic aimed only at rebel slaveholders while keeping Loyalist-owned captives enslaved.

passage.bullet: Thomas Jefferson's 1776 Declaration proclaimed all men equal with natural rights to life and liberty
Forty-one of fifty-six Philadelphia signatories personally enslaved human beings, including Jefferson himself
Half a million African Americans remained legally enslaved → exposed a stark contradiction at birth

context.bullet: Jefferson drew on John Locke's natural rights philosophy while protecting Virginia's tobacco slave economy
Enslaved Africans such as Phillis Wheatley and Massachusetts petitioners immediately used 1776 language against slavery

stems.stem: Meeting in Philadelphia in July 1776, ____________ drafted a declaration claiming ____________ possessed rights to life and liberty.
Yet these words concealed a deep contradiction because ____________ of the fifty-six signatories personally ____________.
Across the thirteen colonies, roughly ____________ remained in chattel bondage without legal freedom.

lesson_5.watch_out: Do not assume people in 1776 failed to notice this hypocrisy—British critics like Samuel Johnson and African American petitioners immediately pointed out the contradiction.

passage.bullet: Continental forces defeated General Burgoyne at Saratoga in October 1777 → proved rebels could win
King Louis XVI entered the war as America's formal ally, supplying troops and warships
Britain diverted warships from North America → prioritized defending rich Jamaican and Caribbean sugar islands

context.bullet: Humiliated in the Seven Years' War, Bourbon France sought revenge by splitting Britain's Atlantic empire
Spain and the Dutch Republic soon joined France → stretched the Royal Navy across oceans

stems.stem: Defeating General Burgoyne in October 1777 convinced ____________ to commit French armies and warships as formal allies.
Once France threatened the West Indies, London diverted vital naval squadrons to protect ____________.
Fighting a worldwide maritime war left British forces in North America short of ____________.

lesson_5.watch_out: To eighteenth-century British ministers, tiny Caribbean sugar islands like Jamaica generated far greater customs wealth than all thirteen mainland colonies combined.

passage.bullet: Lord Cornwallis fortified the coastal Yorktown peninsula in Virginia, relying on Royal Navy supply
French Admiral de Grasse sealed Chesapeake Bay by sea → blocked British rescue and supplies
Washington's Franco-American artillery pounded British trenches → forced 8,000 redcoats to surrender in October 1781

context.bullet: Losing temporary command of American waters proved fatal for an army supplied across the Atlantic
Yorktown broke Parliamentary support for war in London → brought down Lord North's ministry

stems.stem: Camped on a Virginia peninsula, Cornwallis lost his escape route when ____________ sealed off ____________.
Meanwhile, ____________ combined American and French troops by land to bombard British defences with heavy artillery.
Cut off from reinforcements, ____________ surrendered on 19 October 1781, ending major mainland fighting.

lesson_5.watch_out: George Washington could not have trapped Cornwallis alone—French Admiral de Grasse's fleet at Chesapeake Bay and thousands of regular French siege troops were decisive.

passage.bullet: Commander Sir Guy Carleton honoured wartime promises → refused to return 3,000 Black Loyalists
Clerks recorded each person in the Book of Negroes ledger and issued freedom certificates
Evacuees sailed from New York to Nova Scotia → many later founded Freetown, Sierra Leone

context.bullet: George Washington demanded escaped captives back at New York → Carleton offered compensation instead
Losing thirteen colonies in 1783 shifted Britain's imperial focus eastward toward Bengal and India

stems.stem: After the 1783 Paris treaty recognized American independence, British commander ____________ protected 3,000 Black Loyalists in New York.
Military clerks registered families in the ____________ ledger before boarding evacuation ships bound for ____________.
Facing harsh winters and broken land promises in Canada, many settlers later sailed on to found ____________.

lesson_5.watch_out: Freedom in Nova Scotia brought harsh winters, poor soil, and racial discrimination, leading over a thousand Black Loyalists to relocate again in 1792 to found Freetown in Sierra Leone.
